fields.independence_analysis: Three source groups bear on this identity question. First, the 1850 census (src_001) — a government enumeration recorded by a Schuylkill County enumerator in the summer of 1850. Second, the 1860 census (src_003) — a government enumeration recorded by a different enumerator a decade later; as an independently created record, it is a separate evidentiary voice, though it likely shares the same household informant (Thomas Flynn or his wife) for reported facts such as age and birthplace. For the question of household composition and residence, however, each enumerator independently witnessed the household, so the two censuses are independent witnesses to Patrick's continuing presence in Thomas Flynn's home. Third, the 1908 death certificate (src_004) — created 58 years after the 1850 census by an attending physician and a son-in-law informant, with no reference to or awareness of either census record. The Ancestry index (src_002) is a derivative of src_001 and does not constitute an independent evidentiary voice. In sum: two independently recorded government censuses corroborate continuous household membership, and a third source — the death certificate — independently names Thomas Flynn as father, having been created through an entirely separate process and informant chain.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, age consistency: Patrick Flynn appears age 5 in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850 and age 15 in the same household in 1860 — a perfectly consistent 10-year interval with no rounding or estimation error. Matching two census ages exactly across a decade with the same household head is a near-impossibility if the two entries recorded different individuals. Second, unbroken household continuity: the same household head (Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County) is associated with Patrick in both census years, providing affirmative evidence of continuous residence — not merely an absence of contradicting records. Third, independent corroboration: the 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, a conclusion reached by a separate informant (the son-in-law) through a separate record-creation process with no access to census data. All three factors converge on the same identification. The alternative candidate — the Patrick Flynn in household 197, age 6 in 1850 — appears in a different family unit and is not connected to Thomas Flynn in any surviving record. The defensible rationale is a combination of (1) uncorroborated single item (no evidence links the household-197 Patrick to Thomas Flynn) and (2) substantially more credible convergent evidence on the confirmed-same-person side.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The identity of the Patrick Flynn in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household is in question because two boys of nearly identical age bear that name in Schuylkill County in 1850 — one in Thomas Flynn's household (age 5, household 84) and one in an unrelated household (age 6, household 197). The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father but does not specify a prior household or census-period address, leaving open, in isolation, which 1850 Patrick Flynn it describes.

The competing evidence is as follows. On one side: the Patrick Flynn in Thomas Flynn's household (a_001) appears in the 1850 census at age 5, reappears in the 1860 census at age 15 in the same Thomas Flynn household (a_009, a_010), and is independently linked to Thomas Flynn by the death certificate's father field (a_013). On the other side: the Patrick Flynn in household 197 is enumerated in a different family unit in 1850 and does not appear in any record connecting him to Thomas Flynn.

Three independently derived lines of evidence positively identify the Thomas Flynn household child as the research subject. The ages are perfectly consistent across the two censuses — age 5 in 1850 and age 15 in 1860, exactly 10 years, with no rounding or discrepancy. The household continuity is unbroken — the same household head (Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County) appears in both census years. And the death certificate, created 58 years later through an entirely separate informant (the son-in-law) and record-creation process, independently names Thomas Flynn as father. This satisfies the standard for positive placement: identity is confirmed by affirmative corroboration across independent sources, not merely by the alternative candidate's absence from later records.

The identity ambiguity arose from ordinary Irish-immigrant demographics. 'Patrick Flynn' was among the most common names in mid-19th-century anthracite Pennsylvania, where Irish coal-mining families concentrated. Finding two boys of the same name in one county simultaneously is entirely expected and does not imply a record error — it is a naming-pool artifact that the multi-record cross-check resolves.
